structure.rationale: The 18 concepts follow the requester's own outline (issue #146), which this pass preserves verbatim rather than re-deriving: six parts moving from the core mental model (server/session/window/pane, first session) through daily fluency (pane workflow, copy mode, long-running jobs), to ownership (config, bindings, status line), to applied developer workflows (projects, SSH, reproducible workspaces — with Elixir/Phoenix and Rust worked examples per the notes), to automation (scripting, plugins, restoration), and finally advanced/team practice (debugging, sharing sessions, and a capstone personal system). Each concept page is expected to follow the same problem -> concept -> hands-on commands -> realistic workflow -> exercise -> common-mistake shape, which is why the shared stylesheet defines .callout variants for key-idea, warning, mistake, and exercise up front. The requester's appendix material (cheat sheet, annotated tmux.conf, bootstrap scripts, migration guide, glossary) is folded into existing pages rather than spawned as separate concepts, per the notes field, to keep the 18-concept structure intact.
structure.audience: Developers who already live in a terminal (shell, editor, git) but have never used tmux, or use it shallowly and want a deliberate, reproducible setup for solo and remote/pair work.

claims.text: tmux is a terminal multiplexer: a single background server process owns any number of sessions, and lightweight clients (terminal windows) attach to a session to display and control it.

A tmux session is persistent: it survives an accidental disconnection (e.g. an ssh connection timing out) or an intentional detach (prefix + d), because the programs running inside it belong to the server process, not to the client that was viewing it.
Detaching leaves the session running in the background; reattaching with `tmux attach` restores the same panes, scrollback, and running foreground jobs exactly as they were left.

tmux was written by Nicholas Marriott and first released in November 2007 under the ISC license, as a cleaner-codebase, BSD-licensed alternative to GNU Screen; it was imported into the OpenBSD base system in 2009 (OpenBSD 4.6).

tmux's session/window/pane hierarchy and its client-server split are what most sharply distinguish it from GNU Screen: tmux had native, layout-preserving vertical and horizontal splits from its first release, while Screen only gained autosaved split layouts much later (Screen 5.0); operations like switching windows are handled server-side in tmux, so every attached client sees the same state.

A terminal emulator's built-in tabs (macOS Terminal.app, GNOME Terminal, Windows Terminal, etc.) are owned by the terminal application's own process — there is no separate server, so quitting or crashing that application ends every shell inside its tabs at once, with no detach/reattach step available.

iTerm2's tmux integration mode (`tmux -CC`) attaches to a tmux session but renders its windows and panes as native iTerm2 tabs and split panes, so the session is still owned and kept alive by the tmux server while the client gets a native window-manager feel.

snippets.code:
tmux new -s work      # start a new named session
tmux attach -t work    # reattach to it later (any client, any machine with access)
# inside tmux: prefix (Ctrl-b) then d   -> detach, leaving it running
snippets.note: verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

pitfalls: Assuming tmux only matters over SSH: the same server-owned persistence also protects local work from a crashed or accidentally-closed terminal app, an IDE restart, or a laptop reboot.

Confusing 'close the terminal window' with 'end the session': closing the surrounding terminal app just drops a client — the tmux server and its session keep running in the background and can be reattached; typing `exit` in every pane of that session, or `tmux kill-session`, is what actually ends it.
Expecting an IDE's built-in terminal panel to behave like tmux: it is tied to the editor process's lifetime, so closing or crashing the IDE takes every job in it down with no reattach option.

claims.text: tmux is installed from the OS package manager on every mainstream platform: `sudo apt install tmux` (Debian/Ubuntu), `brew install tmux` (macOS via Homebrew), `sudo dnf install tmux` (Fedora), `sudo pacman -S tmux` (Arch); `tmux -V` prints the installed version to confirm.
`tmux new -s NAME` (short for `new-session -s NAME`) creates a new session named NAME and immediately attaches the current terminal to it as a client.
If `-s` is omitted, tmux assigns the session an automatic numeric name starting at 0 (then 1, 2, ...) instead of a memorable one, which makes it harder to target later with `attach -t`.
The default prefix key is Ctrl-b: nearly every tmux command from inside a session is invoked by pressing Ctrl-b, releasing it, then pressing a single command key (e.g. Ctrl-b then d).
Detaching (prefix d, or running `tmux detach-client`) disconnects the client from the session without ending any process inside it; the session keeps running on the server.

`tmux ls` (short for `list-sessions`) lists every session on the server with its window count, creation time, and marks the currently-attached session; `tmux attach -t NAME` (or `tmux a -t NAME`) reattaches to a specific one by name, while `tmux attach` with no `-t` attaches to the most recently used session, not a chosen one.

`tmux new -A -s NAME` is idempotent: it attaches to the session NAME if it already exists, or creates it if it doesn't, which makes it safe to bind as a single 'go to my session' command run from any shell startup or launcher. The -A flag was added in tmux 1.8 (2013).
`tmux kill-session -t NAME` ends a session outright (kills every process inside it), which is different from detaching (prefix d), which merely stops watching it.

tmux tracks whether the current shell is already inside a session via the $TMUX environment variable it sets on attach; running `tmux` again from inside an existing session tries to nest and fails with 'sessions should be nested with care, unset $TMUX to force' rather than silently creating a confusing session-inside-a-session.

The default status line sits at the bottom of the terminal: the left side shows the current session name in brackets, the middle lists the session's windows by index with the active one marked, and the right side shows the host name and clock — all customizable later, but present unmodified from the first session onward.

snippets.code:
# pick one for your platform, then confirm
sudo apt install tmux        # Debian / Ubuntu
brew install tmux            # macOS (Homebrew)
sudo dnf install tmux        # Fedora
sudo pacman -S tmux          # Arch
tmux -V                       # -> tmux 3.x

tmux new -s work        # create + attach a session named "work"
# ...work happens...
# Ctrl-b, release, then d   -> detach, session keeps running

tmux ls                  # -> work: 1 windows (created ...) (attached)
tmux attach -t work      # or: tmux a -t work

tmux kill-session -t work   # ends it outright, unlike detaching
snippets.note: the full first-session loop: create, detach, list, reattach, end

snippets.code: tmux new -A -s work   # attaches to "work" if it exists, creates it if not
snippets.note: idempotent create-or-attach, safe to run repeatedly

pitfalls: Skipping -s and getting a numeric session name (0, 1, 2, ...): it works, but weeks later `tmux ls` is the only way to remember what's what — name every session on purpose.

Running `tmux` again from inside an already-attached session tries to nest and fails with 'sessions should be nested with care, unset $TMUX to force'; detach first (prefix d) and reattach, rather than fighting the warning.
Assuming `tmux attach` with no `-t` will ask which session to open: it silently attaches to the most-recently-used one, which is the wrong session as soon as more than one exists.

Reading the status line's session name in brackets as a window title, or the window list in the middle as a list of sessions — the three zones (session / windows / host+clock) are easy to conflate on a first look.

claims.text: tmux's object model is a strict hierarchy: one server process holds any number of sessions; each session holds one or more windows; each window holds one or more panes, which are the actual shells/programs running side by side inside a window.

A window is a single full-screen layout (of one or more panes) shown at one time; a session is really just a named list of windows plus which one is currently active, and a client only ever displays one window of one session at a time.

Objects are addressed with a target string of the form session:window.pane (e.g. work:1.2 = pane 2 of window 1 in session work); if a target is left partially or fully unqualified, tmux fills in the current session/window/pane, which is convenient interactively but should be written fully qualified in scripts.

By default, window and pane indexes are zero-based (the first window is 0, the first pane in it is 0); this is a common surprise for people used to 1-based counting, and is controlled by the base-index and pane-base-index session options (set later, in configuration).

prefix c runs new-window, creating a new window in the current session and switching to it; prefix , runs command-prompt to rename the current window; prefix & runs kill-window (with a confirmation prompt) to close the current window and everything in it.

Window navigation: prefix n / prefix p move to the next/previous window; prefix 0-9 jumps directly to that window index; prefix w opens an interactive, searchable list of all windows to choose from; prefix l jumps back to the last (previously) selected window, a fast toggle between two windows.

prefix % runs split-window -h, splitting the current pane into a left and right pair (a vertical dividing line); prefix " runs split-window -v, splitting it into a top and bottom pair (a horizontal dividing line) — the -h/-v flags name the split line's orientation, not the resulting pane arrangement, which is the single most common point of confusion for new users.

Pane navigation and management: prefix + arrow key moves focus to the pane in that direction; prefix o cycles focus to the next pane; prefix q briefly overlays each pane with its number, and pressing that number jumps straight to it; prefix x runs kill-pane (with confirmation) to close just that pane, leaving the rest of the window intact; prefix z runs resize-pane -Z to toggle zooming the current pane to fill the whole window (and back).
Closing the last pane in a window closes the window; closing the last window in a session ends the session (and, if it was the last session on the server, the server itself exits).

prefix ! runs break-pane, promoting the current pane out into its own new window; prefix { and prefix } run swap-pane -U / swap-pane -D to swap the current pane's position with the previous/next pane in the window's layout order, without changing focus.

A pane's program exiting (e.g. the shell inside it exits) closes that pane automatically; tmux does not ask for confirmation in that case the way it does for prefix x, since the process simply ended on its own.

snippets.code:
# from the command line (outside tmux), fully-qualified targets:
tmux new-window -t work -n build       # add a window named "build" to session work
tmux select-window -t work:2           # jump to window index 2 in session work
tmux split-window -h -t work:1         # split window 1's active pane left/right
tmux select-pane -t work:1.2           # focus pane 2 of window 1
tmux kill-window -t work:2             # close window 2 and everything in it
tmux list-windows -t work              # show every window in session work
tmux list-panes -t work:1              # show every pane in window 1
snippets.note: verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

snippets.code:
prefix c        new-window              prefix &   kill-window (confirm)
prefix ,        rename-window           prefix l   last-window (toggle)
prefix n / p    next / previous window  prefix w   choose-window (list)
prefix 0-9      select window by index

prefix %        split-window -h  (left | right)
prefix "        split-window -v  (top / bottom)
prefix arrows   move focus one pane over
prefix o        cycle focus to next pane
prefix q        flash pane numbers, press one to jump
prefix x        kill-pane (confirm)      prefix z   zoom/unzoom pane
prefix !        break-pane to new window prefix {}  swap-pane prev/next
snippets.note: the default (unmodified) key table; all still Ctrl-b as the second key of prefix, then the listed key

pitfalls: Assuming % gives a horizontal (stacked) split and " gives a vertical (side-by-side) one — it's the reverse: the flag names the dividing line's orientation, not the pane layout, and this trips up almost everyone at first.
Typing 1, 2, 3... expecting to jump to the "first" window with prefix 1 and landing on the second one instead, because window/pane indexes are zero-based by default.

Confusing a new window (prefix c — a whole new full-screen layout, still the same session) with a new pane (prefix % or " — a split inside the current window) — reaching for the wrong one wastes screen space or fragments work that should have stayed in one place.
Running prefix x or prefix & out of habit and blowing past the confirmation prompt without reading it, killing a pane/window with unsaved work in it.

claims.text: resize-pane (bound by default to prefix + an arrow key held with a modifier) changes a pane's dimensions without changing the layout's shape otherwise: prefix then Ctrl-Up/Down/Left/Right grows or shrinks the current pane by one cell in that direction, and prefix then Meta(Alt)-Up/Down/Left/Right does the same in five-cell steps for a bigger adjustment.

The Ctrl-arrow and Meta-arrow resize bindings are repeatable: after pressing prefix once, tmux keeps accepting the same key (held or pressed again) for the repeat-time window (500ms by default) without requiring the prefix again, so holding Ctrl and tapping an arrow several times resizes in one fluid motion instead of one prefix per cell.

resize-pane also accepts an explicit target and amount from the command line or command prompt, e.g. `resize-pane -t work:1.2 -R 10` grows pane 2 of window 1 ten cells to the right, and `resize-pane -Z` toggles zooming the current pane to fill the whole window (the same operation bound to prefix z).

tmux ships five built-in pane layouts, cycled through with select-layout: even-horizontal (panes spread evenly left-to-right, side by side), even-vertical (panes spread evenly top-to-bottom, stacked), main-horizontal (one large pane across the top, the rest in a row underneath), main-vertical (one large pane on the left, the rest stacked in a column on the right), and tiled (panes arranged in as even a grid as the pane count allows).

prefix Space runs next-layout, cycling through the five built-in layouts in order and reflowing every pane in the current window to fit the chosen layout, which is faster than hand-resizing a layout you've fought into a wrong shape.

Each built-in layout can also be selected directly, either from the command prompt (`:select-layout tiled`) or via the default bindings prefix Alt-1 through prefix Alt-5, mapped in order to even-horizontal, even-vertical, main-horizontal, main-vertical, and tiled.

prefix Ctrl-o runs rotate-window, which rotates the panes of the current window forward through the positions of the active layout (each pane's content moves to the next slot) without changing which layout is in effect or which pane has focus's relative position.

The synchronize-panes window option, toggled with `setw synchronize-panes on` (and off again the same way), makes every keystroke typed into the active pane get sent to every other pane in that window simultaneously -- not just visible characters but backspaces and cursor movement too -- so one typed command runs identically across all of them at once.

join-pane (and its mirror move-pane) relocates an existing pane from one window into another, taking `-s` (source pane) and `-t` (target window or pane) plus an optional `-h`/`-v` to say whether it joins as a horizontal or vertical split; this differs from break-pane (already covered), which does the opposite -- pulling a pane out into a brand-new window.

Setting `set -g mouse on` in tmux.conf (or running `:set -g mouse on` for the current session) turns on mouse support: clicking a pane focuses it, clicking a window's name in the status line switches to it, dragging a pane border resizes the panes on either side of it, and the scroll wheel scrolls a pane's history -- all without leaving the keyboard-driven bindings intact.

snippets.code:
prefix Ctrl-arrow    resize-pane, 1 cell   (repeatable within repeat-time)
prefix Meta-arrow     resize-pane, 5 cells  (repeatable within repeat-time)
prefix Space          next-layout           (cycle the 5 built-in layouts)
prefix Alt-1..Alt-5   select-layout directly: even-h, even-v, main-h, main-v, tiled
prefix Ctrl-o         rotate-window         (rotate pane positions forward)
snippets.note: default bindings, verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

snippets.code:
# resize pane 2 of window 1 in session work, 10 cells to the right, from outside
tmux resize-pane -t work:1.2 -R 10

# jump straight to a named layout instead of hand-resizing
tmux select-layout -t work:1 tiled

# move a pane living in window 2 into window 1, as a new right-hand split
tmux join-pane -h -s work:2.1 -t work:1
snippets.note: verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

snippets.code:
# run the same command on three hosts side by side
tmux new -s fleet
Ctrl-b %
Ctrl-b %
# ssh into three different hosts, one per pane, then:
Ctrl-b :setw synchronize-panes on
# type once -- it goes to all three panes at once
sudo apt update
# turn it back off before doing anything pane-specific
Ctrl-b :setw synchronize-panes off

pitfalls: Leaving synchronize-panes on after the job it was turned on for is done: the next command typed -- including something destructive like an rm or a service restart -- goes to every pane in the window at once, not just the one you're looking at. Turn it off the moment the parallel task is finished, and treat the status line (which tmux marks while it's active) as a thing to actually glance at.

Hand-resizing panes one Ctrl-arrow tap at a time when a built-in layout already matches the shape wanted: prefix Space (or a direct prefix Alt-N) reflows the whole window in one step and is almost always faster than nudging borders into place.

Confusing join-pane's -h/-v with split-window's: both use -h for a left/right (side-by-side) result and -v for a top/bottom (stacked) result, but because join-pane operates across windows it's easy to mistype the target and join into the wrong window's layout -- `list-windows` first if unsure.

Turning on `mouse on` and then fighting it when trying to select and copy multi-line text the OS way: with mouse mode active, tmux's own click-drag takes over pane selection and copy mode instead of the terminal's native text selection, which surprises people expecting their usual triple-click-to-select-a-line behavior (the fix -- holding a modifier key while dragging, e.g. Option/Shift depending on terminal -- is terminal-specific and worth knowing before it's needed).
